title: The poor people's Bible
hookLine: colored windows told Bible stories to people who couldn't read

lines: COLORED LIGHT ON A STONE FLOOR.
cards: Late afternoon, and a patch of blue and red light slides slowly across a stone floor. Follow it up to where it comes from, and there's a window high in the wall, made of small pieces of colored glass.
Look closer, and the colors become people. A man in a boat. A woman at a well.
A shepherd carrying a sheep on his shoulders. A whole story, told in light, pane by pane, from the bottom of the window to the top.

teach.h: COLOR IN THE GLASS, FACES PAINTED ON.
teach.b: Stained glass gets its color as the glass is made.
Then the details, faces, hands, the folds of a robe, are painted on with dark paint and fired so they hold, and lead strips join the pieces like the lines in a coloring book.
In the great churches of the middle ages, windows like these told the Bible's stories, and the lives of the saints, to people who couldn't read.
A pope, Gregory the Great, wrote to a bishop who had smashed the pictures in his church.
Don't destroy them, Gregory told him: what writing gives to those who can read, a picture gives to those who can't. Some people later called windows like these the poor people's Bible.
Some historians wonder how much anyone could make out of a window that high, but even from the floor, the light did its work.
Windows often paired stories, one from the Old Testament beside one from the New, so that Jonah coming out of the fish sits near Jesus rising from the tomb. Often you read them from the bottom up.
John writes, in the King James Bible, "And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not."
A stained glass window is dark from the outside. You only see its story from inside, when the sun comes through. Christians haven't all loved these windows.
In some times and places, reformers broke them, believing images drew worship away from God. Other Protestants kept them and made new ones, and churches of different traditions use them still.

how: Stained glass windows still tell Bible stories in churches of different traditions, and churches sometimes hold tours or talks that walk people through a window's story from bottom to top.

games.q: you're Gregory the Great. a bishop writes that he has smashed the pictures in his church so no one worships them. what do you tell him?
o: don't destroy them: a picture gives to those who can't read what writing gives to readers.
games.why: Gregory told the bishop not to destroy them: pictures teach those who cannot read.

practice: If you can, find something colored and clear, a bottle, a glass of juice, a colored jar, even a phone screen set to a single color, and hold it up to a lamp or a window.
Watch the color the light makes, and notice that the glass does nothing on its own; it waits for the light. If you pray, give thanks for the light; if you don't, simply watch it.

wordCard.voice: Stained glass. Colored glass, painted and leaded into windows that tell the Bible's stories in light, once called the poor people's Bible.

orig.note: Latin: the Bible of the poor, a name later given to picture Bibles and windows like these.
